meta.titre: Informal Fallacies: how to identify, explain and illustrate faulty reasoning

sections.contenu_markdown: During a school election campaign, a candidate for class captain says: "Do not vote for my rival, because he failed Mathematics last year." The crowd applauds, yet nothing has been said about what the rival would do as captain. In the same way, advertisements, political speeches and market-place arguments are full of reasoning that looks strong and is not. The paper often gives a short passage and asks you to identify, explain and illustrate the fallacy committed, so you need exact names, exact definitions and your own examples.

items: An argument is a set of premises offered as reasons for a conclusion.
A good argument has relevant, acceptable premises that give enough support for its conclusion.
A formal fallacy is an error in the pattern of an argument, while an informal fallacy is an error of content, relevance or language.

sections.titre: Fallacies of relevance, presumption, induction and ambiguity
sections.contenu_markdown:
### What a fallacy is
A **fallacy** is a mistake in reasoning that makes an argument unsound or unconvincing although it may seem persuasive. A fallacious argument may even have a true conclusion: the fault lies in the reasoning, not in the conclusion.

### Main informal fallacies
| Group | Fallacy | The mistake | Short example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Relevance | Argument against the person (ad hominem) | attacks the speaker instead of the argument | Reject her budget because she is young. |
| Relevance | Appeal to force (ad baculum) | a threat replaces a reason | Agree with me or you lose your job. |
| Relevance | Appeal to pity (ad misericordiam) | pity replaces evidence | Raise my mark because I cried. |
| Relevance | Appeal to the people (ad populum) | popularity treated as proof | Everybody buys it, so it is good. |
| Relevance | Appeal to ignorance | lack of disproof is taken as proof | Nobody has shown it false, so it is true. |
| Relevance | Appeal to unqualified authority | an authority outside his field is quoted | A footballer is cited on medicine. |
| Relevance | Irrelevant conclusion | proves something other than the point at issue | Argues that crime is bad when the issue is how to stop it. |
| Presumption | Begging the question | the conclusion is assumed in the premises | He is honest because he never lies. |
| Presumption | Complex question | one question hides an unproved assumption | Have you stopped cheating in tests? |
| Presumption | False cause | one event is taken as the cause because it came first | The cock crowed, then the sun rose. |
| Presumption | Accident | a general rule is applied to a case where it does not fit | Free speech is a right, so a student may shout during an examination. |
| Induction | Hasty generalisation | a conclusion about all or most from too few or atypical cases | Two rude waiters, so all waiters are rude. |
| Ambiguity | Equivocation | one word changes meaning inside the argument | A bank is a place of money; a river has a bank, so a river has money. |

Group names vary slightly between textbooks. Learn the definition and give your own illustration.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question gives a passage and asks you to identify, explain and illustrate the fallacy committed.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Use four steps and spend one mark on each. (1) **Identify**: find the conclusion and the reason, test the reason, and give the exact name. (2) **Explain**: define the fallacy and show why the reason does not support the conclusion in this passage. (3) **Illustrate**: write a new example of your own, not a copy of the passage. (4) **Close**: say what a sound argument would require.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks for the value of the study of fallacies, or asks you to discuss it.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Give three or four reasons, each with a short explanation. We study fallacies to avoid them in our own reasoning, to detect them in the arguments of others, to resist manipulation in politics and advertising, and to train the habit of asking for reasons. They also improve clear writing in examinations and in daily debate.

sections.enonce_markdown: A school council member says: "The Minister claims that the new tax will help rural schools. But the Minister is wealthy and has never taught, so his tax plan must be rejected." Identify, explain and illustrate the fallacy committed.

etapes.action: Find the conclusion and the reason given for it.
etapes.justification: The conclusion is that the tax plan must be rejected. The only reason is that the Minister is wealthy and has never taught.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Reason: facts about the Minister. Nothing is said about the tax itself.

etapes.action: Test whether the reason is relevant.
etapes.justification: A good reason against a tax plan would concern its costs, its effects or its fairness. The wealth and the career of its author do not tell us whether the plan works.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The reason is irrelevant to the conclusion.

etapes.justification: An argument that rejects a claim by attacking the person who makes it, instead of examining the claim, is the argument against the person.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The fallacy is **ad hominem** (circumstantial: it points to the Minister's situation).

etapes.justification: A plan can be good even when its author is rich or inexperienced, and a bad plan can come from a wise person. Truth and soundness do not depend on who speaks.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The premise gives no support to the conclusion, so the argument is unsound.

etapes.justification: A good illustration is built on the same pattern with different content.
etapes.resultat_markdown: "Do not accept the doctor's advice to drink more water: he is a smoker." The doctor's habits do not show that the advice is wrong.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The council member commits the fallacy of the **argument against the person (ad hominem)**: he attacks the Minister's circumstances instead of the content of the plan. A sound reply would show, with evidence, that the tax would not help rural schools or would harm them in some other way.

items.erreur_markdown: Writing that an argument is a fallacy because its conclusion is false.
items.pourquoi_faux: A fallacy is a fault of reasoning. A false conclusion may come from a false premise in a valid argument, and a fallacious argument can have a true conclusion.
items.correction_markdown: Say what is wrong with the link between the reason and the conclusion, for example that the reason is irrelevant or that the sample is too small.

items.erreur_markdown: Naming the fallacy but giving no explanation and no example.
items.pourquoi_faux: A question with the verbs identify, explain and illustrate has marks for each task. A bare name earns only the first.
items.correction_markdown: Write the name, a definition applied to the passage, and a new example of your own.

items.erreur_markdown: Treating every criticism of a person as ad hominem.
items.pourquoi_faux: It is relevant to question a witness's honesty when the case depends on the witness's word. The fallacy occurs only when the personal attack replaces an answer to the argument.
items.correction_markdown: Check whether the personal fact bears on the claim. If it does not, the fallacy is present.

items.erreur_markdown: Mixing up accident and hasty generalisation.
items.pourquoi_faux: Accident applies a general rule to a special case where the rule does not fit; hasty generalisation moves from a few cases to a general rule. They run in opposite directions.
items.correction_markdown: Ask which way the reasoning goes: from rule to exception (accident) or from cases to rule (hasty generalisation).

items.erreur_markdown: Using 'begging the question' to mean 'making us ask the question'.
items.pourquoi_faux: In logic it means assuming the conclusion in the premises, which is also called circular reasoning.
items.correction_markdown: Look for a premise that only repeats the conclusion in other words.

items.enonce_markdown: Name the fallacy: *Half of the class is using this brand of calculator, so it must be the best.* Explain in two sentences.
items.solution_markdown: The fallacy is the **appeal to the people (ad populum)**. The number of users shows popularity, not quality, so the reason is irrelevant to the conclusion. A sound argument would compare accuracy, price and durability.

items.enonce_markdown: Name the fallacy and explain it: *No one has proved that the old well is not haunted, so it is haunted.* Then rewrite the claim so that it no longer commits the fallacy.
items.solution_markdown: The fallacy is the **appeal to ignorance**: absence of disproof is taken as proof. The same reasoning could prove the opposite whenever nobody has proved a claim true. A non-fallacious version: *We have no evidence either way, so we cannot say whether the well is haunted.*

items.enonce_markdown: Identify the fallacy in each argument and explain it in one or two sentences. (a) *A feather is light. What is light cannot be dark. So a feather cannot be dark.* (b) *Our school newspaper always tells the truth, because it says so in its own editorial.* (c) *The generator broke down after the new teacher arrived, so the new teacher caused the breakdown.* Then give two reasons why the study of fallacies is useful.
items.solution_markdown: (a) **Equivocation**: light means not heavy in the first premise and not dark in the second, so the word changes meaning. (b) **Begging the question** (circular reasoning): the claim that the newspaper is truthful rests only on its own statement that it is truthful. (c) **False cause** (post hoc): coming after an event is taken as being caused by it, with no evidence of a link. Usefulness: the study of fallacies helps us avoid faulty reasoning in our own work, and it helps us detect and resist manipulation in political speeches and advertisements.

items_markdown: A fallacy is an error of reasoning; the fault lies in the link between reason and conclusion, not in whether the conclusion is true.
Learn each fallacy by its name, its definition and one example of your own, grouped as relevance, presumption, induction and ambiguity.
Answer identify, explain and illustrate in three separate parts: the name, the reason it fails in the passage, and a new example.
Do not confuse accident with hasty generalisation: one applies a rule to an exception, the other builds a rule from too few cases.
We study fallacies to avoid them, to detect them in others and to resist manipulation.
